clinical_knowledge.topic: Chronic Idiopathic Urticaria evaluation and management
core_concepts: Chronic idiopathic (spontaneous) urticaria is defined by daily or near-daily hives for six weeks or more without an identifiable external trigger, despite a thorough history and workup.
A subset of cases has an autoimmune component (autoantibodies against IgE or its high-affinity receptor on mast cells), and coexisting autoimmune thyroid disease is more common in this population.
First-line treatment is scheduled (not PRN) non-sedating second-generation antihistamines, up-titrated to up to four times the standard dose before escalating therapy.
Individual welts should resolve within 24 hours without bruising or scarring; lesions lasting longer or leaving marks suggest an alternative diagnosis such as urticarial vasculitis.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: recurrent hives daily for more than 6 weeks

Key HPI features: A 32-year-old female presents to the clinic with recurrent hives daily for more than 6 weeks. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Transient, blanching wheals may be seen during an active flare; none present between episodes, with no bruising or residual pigmentation from prior welts.
common_misconceptions: Ordering extensive allergy panels, which are rarely helpful since chronic idiopathic urticaria is not usually triggered by a specific allergen.
Treating antihistamines only as needed rather than on a scheduled, up-titrated basis.
Overlooking screening for underlying autoimmune thyroid disease, which is more prevalent in this population.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to chronic inducible urticaria (identifiable physical trigger) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Welts lasting over 24 hours or leaving bruising.
management_principles: Start a scheduled (not PRN) non-sedating second-generation antihistamine, up-titrating to up to 4x standard dose if needed.
Check TSH and consider screening for underlying autoimmune thyroid disease.
Consider omalizumab for antihistamine-refractory disease after specialist evaluation.
Refer to Allergy/Immunology if symptoms persist despite an adequate antihistamine trial.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

learning_objectives: Recognize the clinical presentation and diagnostic criteria of chronic idiopathic (spontaneous) urticaria
Distinguish chronic idiopathic urticaria from chronic inducible urticaria and urticarial vasculitis
Select the appropriate stepwise antihistamine dosing strategy and relevant screening tests for chronic urticaria

teaching.one_liner: Daily hives for more than six weeks with no identifiable cause despite investigation — managed with escalating antihistamine doses.
red_flags: Welts lasting over 24 hours or leaving bruising

must_ask.say: How many weeks has this been happening?
Is it happening daily, or does it come and go?
Have you noticed any pattern — food, stress, temperature?
Any thyroid problems, fatigue, or joint pain?
What antihistamine dose are you on, and is it controlling it?
